explain.say: On 20 November 1945, in the Palace of Justice in Nuremberg, twenty-one of the most senior surviving Nazi leaders sat in the dock. The chief American prosecutor, Robert Jackson, said that the victors, still wounded, had chosen law over revenge. Look at the timeline from these trials to today's courts.

explain.say: Look at the map. Nuremberg was chosen partly because its courthouse survived the bombing, and it had been the city of Nazi rallies and the 1935 race laws. In Tokyo, from May 1946, the International Military Tribunal for the Far East had judges from eleven countries, including India, the Philippines and China. Why might the place of a trial matter?

See the charges. Conspiracy, crimes against peace, meaning planning a war of aggression, war crimes like killing prisoners, and crimes against humanity like deportation and extermination. The lawyer Raphael Lemkin had coined the word genocide in 1944, and in 1948 the UN made it a crime. Which charge would be hardest to prove, do you think?

explain.say: Now the verdicts at Nuremberg on 1 October 1946. Of twenty-two defendants judged, twelve were sentenced to death, three to life in prison, four to prison terms, and three were acquitted. In Tokyo, seven, including the wartime prime minister Tōjō Hideki, were sentenced to death and sixteen to life. Why do you think acquittals mattered?

Now the debate. Critics called it victor's justice: Allied acts were never judged, and the Indian judge Radhabinod Pal dissented at Tokyo. Defenders say it put evidence on record and founded international criminal law, leading to the ICC in 2002. Thoughtful work. Challenge: decide what would make such a court fair.

faq.a: Trials of leading Nazis before the International Military Tribunal set up by the USA, Britain, France and the Soviet Union. The main trial ran from November 1945 to October 1946; later trials judged doctors, judges, industrialists and others.

faq.q: What crimes were tried at Nuremberg?
faq.a: Four counts: conspiracy, crimes against peace (planning and waging aggressive war), war crimes (breaking the laws of war, such as killing prisoners) and crimes against humanity (murder, extermination, deportation and persecution of civilians).
Raphael Lemkin, a Polish-Jewish lawyer, coined the word genocide in 1944. The UN Genocide Convention, adopted on 9 December 1948, made genocide a crime under international law.

The International Military Tribunal for the Far East, from 1946 to 1948, tried 28 Japanese leaders. Judges came from eleven nations. Seven were sentenced to death, including Tōjō Hideki, and sixteen to life imprisonment. Emperor Hirohito was not charged.
asks: Why was Emperor Hirohito not tried?

faq.q: Were the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials victor's justice?
faq.a: Critics note that only the defeated were tried, Allied actions such as the bombing of cities were not judged, and crimes against peace were new law. Justice Radhabinod Pal dissented at Tokyo. Defenders reply that the trials gave defendants lawyers, recorded vast evidence and founded modern international criminal law.

facts: The main Nuremberg trial opened on 20 November 1945.
Nuremberg verdicts were given on 1 October 1946: twelve death sentences and three acquittals.
The UN adopted the Genocide Convention on 9 December 1948.

quiz.say: Of 22 defendants judged at Nuremberg, 3 were acquitted. How many were found guilty?
quiz.why: 22 minus 3 acquitted leaves 19 convicted: 12 death sentences, 3 life terms and 4 prison terms.

wrong.1: Twelve were the death sentences only.

quiz.say: Which judge dissented at the Tokyo trial?
quiz.show: The famous dissent at Tokyo came from…
quiz.why: Justice Pal argued the trial was victor's justice and would have acquitted all defendants.

wrong.1: Robert Jackson was the US chief prosecutor at Nuremberg.
wrong.2: Lemkin was a lawyer who coined genocide, not a judge at Tokyo.
